title: No more selling fees from May 2026
body:
O.P.
So where do they get their income which is declining badly the last 3 years?

[User #10400215551 postscluster2Whirlpool Forums Addict] this post was edited
I sell over $25k per year on eBay and as far as I can see the changes for me are:
- Increase of international fees from 1.1% to 3% extra - Buyer protection included for free - All other fees don't change
It also looks like I won't be forced use ebay's labels. This is a really big point for me as I use untracked letters for small/cheap items and MyPost Business for everything else.
Will buyers see a 'protection fee' as a separate item on their invoice? Right now they don't have a clue what the seller pays in terms of fees. Will all prices rise by the protection fee on eBay? Mine won't, AFAIK, as the protection fee is free for me.
If a buyer pays a 'protection fee' on eBay, will I be forced to use tracked postage? I really hope not, otherwise I will have to remove hundreds of listings when postage climbs from $1.70 to ~$8.
These changes are a real mess and quite honestly a headache.
As for the OP's question on where does eBay get its income from? Me. I've paid over $6k in fees last year. Also this new buyer protection fee regime is being touted as fee free selling for sub $25k sellers, but it's just shifting fees around while lowering them a bit.

[User #8443291322 postsAnarkikOrteesteConvinced of a Soylent future.Whirlpool Enthusiast] natulya writes...
Sendle were in bankruptcy and stopped all services recently
Had to investigate that and looks like Sendle operated under bankruptcy administration since 2022 then just last month the business was liquidated and ceased operating. When I Googled 'Ebay carrier partners' the AI slop I always skim past has the old information with Sendle at the top as Ebay's preferred carrier.
Ebay had misleading information. I was interested in the "Free fees selling" and actually read the linked information page thoroughly just the other day. Certain it informed that you must use Ebay Labels for postage with their 'Carrier Partners'. The 'Carrier Partners' link said they use Sendle, AusPost, Couriers Please or others, also you could get a QR code to arrange a Sendle parcel pickup. That's fresh in my mind but I've checked that page just now and it's been modified (I think) to only mention AusPost as a carrier partner.
When you see Ebay's crazy idea that with seller 'free fees' but buyers will now be paying a 'buyer protection fee' on top of the price and postage, Ebay is surely in it's death throws.
With the near non-existent buyers and low traffic, I don't follow my live listings on GT or Ebay at all. Just 1 scammer on GT trying to get an email or phone number to take the messages off GT, they deleted the fresh (obvious scammer) account with "Fraud detection". Ebay auctions sometimes sell for 1st bid only or mostly 'passed in' and Buy it Now's occasionally sell or lowballers message even though "Best/Worst Offers" is not enabled. I just troll them and then block from further messages/purchases. I really don't want to join Zuckerberg's Marketplace just to sell some collectables locally, not international.
[User #654423792 postsgmailaccountWhirlpool Forums Addict] You have to wonder who or what at eBay in their commercial team is thinking things through.
At its core, eBay is a marketplace that connects buyers and sellers together in a platform they design, create and run. If eBay need or want 13.4% of the revenue for that – their model is doomed.
The new concept, to move fees from sellers to buyers – but in reality means sellers need to lower sales costs so the buyer sees actual price points doesn't really solve the core problem which is simply eBays fees are far too high for the value they create or offer buyers or sellers.

[User #8856531382 postssozzled2Whirlpool Enthusiast] I had a quick look at the email I received from eBay today. I buy a lot of goods on eBay by the way: the usual consumables (ink cartridges/toners for my printers; batteries; USB cables) and other items that are available more "conveniently" than in bricks and mortar stores). Most of the stuff I order on eBay costs under $20 and I occasionally splurge—to around $100—on purchases that I wouldn't often buy (e.g. a new wristwatch).
I played with being a seller on eBay once but I decided it just wasn't worth the effort. Most of the things I'd be selling would be second-hand items that are easier sold locally using Facebook Marketplace or Gumtree. However, as a consumer—a buyer—what does the additional "buyer protection" feature (and its associated fees) mean in a practical sense.
Here's the blurb ("courtesy" of eBay):
When purchasing from Australia-based sellers who don't have a Pro plan, the Buyer Protection fee is calculated as:
A flat fee of $0.30 per item, and 8% of the item price up to $20, and 6% of any portion of the item price from $20 to $500, and 4% of any portion of the item price from $500 to $5,000
The reference I quoted above provides a few examples. So, what does this mean when I want to purchase two 4-packs of CR123A batteries for a couple of Arlo security cameras, for instance? When I last bought these things (less than two weeks ago) they cost me $17.45. Applying eBay's new rules, the next time I buy these things (in another three months or thereabouts), assuming the seller hasn't increased the price, they will cost $19.15. That's an increase of just on 9.7%.
Admittedly, the CR123A batteries I'm talking about are unbranded but, compared to the cost of branded—e.g. Energiser—batteries from, say Bunnings or Officeworks (or even Jaycar) all within walking distance from home, it's not even a close race. I'm not sure what kind of added "protection" I'm getting with eBay's new "plan"; it all sounds like a gimmick to me to increase eBay's profits rather than offset its operational costs. Whatever spin one puts on this, it's unlikely to stop be buying stuff on eBay. Comme-çi comme-ça .
